text.t: Cholesterol is the most common steroid, a lipid built from linked carbon rings.
Its formula is C27H46O: 27 carbons and a single oxygen.
All steroids share four linked carbon rings, three with six carbons and one with five.
One OH group sits on the end of the rings, which puts cholesterol in the alcohol family called sterols.
At the other end, cholesterol has a short tail of carbon and hydrogen.
In a cell membrane, cholesterol lies alongside the phospholipids in the membrane's core.

does.t: In the membrane, cholesterol dampens the effect of temperature, keeping the membrane fluid over a wider range of temperatures.
It is also the starting material for steroid hormones such as testosterone and estradiol, for vitamin D and for bile salts that help digest fats.

shape.t: Like other lipids, cholesterol is mostly carbon and hydrogen, so it does not dissolve in water.
Its rings and tail avoid water, so in a membrane it sits alongside the phospholipids in the water-free core.

text.t: Cholesterol is a component of the plasma membrane of animal cells.

wrong.t: High levels of LDL, often called bad cholesterol, may lead to plaque in the arteries and heart disease.
Even so, cholesterol itself is necessary for the body to work properly.

compare.t: From its farthest atom to its farthest atom, cholesterol measures about 1.8 nm.
Palmitic acid, also in this gallery, measures about 2.2 nm.

text.t: The single oxygen, which makes cholesterol a sterol.
The only carbon-to-carbon double bond in cholesterol joins these two ring carbons.
